methods.name: FedRot-LoRA
methods.full_name: Federated LoRA with rotational alignment of client factors
methods.paper_title: FedRot-LoRA: Mitigating Rotational Misalignment in Federated LoRA
methods.formula_latex: h=(W_0+\bar B^{t}\bar A^{t})x,\ \ \bar B^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ \bar A^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\quad \text{client } i \text{ trains } (B_i^t,A_i^t) \text{ starting from } (\bar B^{t-1},\bar A^{t-1});\quad R_i^{t,*}=\arg\min_{R^\top R=I_r,\ \det R>0}\begin{cases}\|R^\top A_i^t-\bar A^{t-1}\|_F^2, & t\ \text{odd}\\ \|B_i^tR-\bar B^{t-1}\|_F^2, & t\ \text{even}\end{cases}\ \ (\text{orthogonal Procrustes, closed form via the SVD of an } r\times r \text{ correlation matrix});\quad R_{i,\mathrm{soft}}^t=\Pi_{SO(r)}\big((1-\lambda)I_r+\lambda R_i^{t,*}\big);\quad \tilde A_i^t=R_{i,\mathrm{soft}}^{t\top}A_i^t,\ \ \tilde B_i^t=B_i^tR_{i,\mathrm{soft}}^t\ \ (\tilde B_i^t\tilde A_i^t=B_i^tA_i^t);\quad \bar A^t=\tfrac1N\textstyle\sum_i\tilde A_i^t,\ \ \bar B^t=\tfrac1N\sum_i\tilde B_i^t;\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen},\ A,B\ \text{trained on clients},\ R\ \text{computed in closed form}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix (per client; same communication as FedIT); } R_i^t\in SO(r)\ \text{is computed, not trained}
methods.locus: LoRA-adapted linear layers in federated fine-tuning (RoBERTa-Large on GLUE; Llama 3-8B on GSM8K and HumanEval), implemented in FederatedScope-LLM
methods.structure: Each client trains a rank-\(r\) LoRA \(\Delta W=BA\). The contribution is the aggregation map: before uploading, each client picks a representative of its factor pair's orbit under the \(SO(r)\) subgroup of the \(GL(r)\) gauge action \((B,A)\mapsto(BR,R^{-1}A)\). The representative is chosen by orthogonal Procrustes against last round's global factors, aligning \(A\) and \(B\) in alternate rounds. The server then averages factors, so the global adapter stays rank \(r\) and \(\bar B\bar A\) approximates \(\tfrac1N\sum_iB_iA_i\) up to the aggregation error \(E^t=\bar B\bar A-\tfrac1N\sum_iB_iA_i\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The global adapter \(\bar B^t\bar A^t\) is an ordinary rank-\(r\) LoRA product and folds into \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: \(\Delta W_0=\bar B^0\bar A^0=0\) (Algorithm 1, line 2; the scalar example in Fig. 2 starts from \(\bar B^0=0\)), so training starts at \(W_0\). Each alignment preserves every client's update exactly, since \(\tilde B_i\tilde A_i=B_iRR^\top A_i=B_iA_i\).
methods.key_idea: Because \((BR)(R^\top A)=BA\) for every rotation \(R\), clients can reach equivalent but rotated factors, and averaging them gives a \(\bar B\bar A\) far from \(\tfrac1N\sum_iB_iA_i\). Fixing this gauge with a closed-form Procrustes rotation toward last round's global factors (softened by \(\lambda\); \(\lambda=0\) is plain FedIT averaging) shrinks the aggregation-error term in the nonconvex convergence bound. It costs \(O(dr^2+r^3)\) per client and adds no communication.
methods.results_note: On GLUE with RoBERTa-Large (\(r=4\), Dirichlet \(h=0.5\), \(N=50\) clients; Table 1), FedRot-LoRA averages 87.34% accuracy versus 82.44% for RoLoRA and 76.80% for FedIT.

relations.note: Plain LoRA factors on each client; only the aggregation changes.
With rotation strength \(\lambda=0\), FedRot-LoRA reduces to FedIT's naive factor-wise averaging (Section 3, after Eq. 6).

FFA-LoRA makes aggregation exact by freezing \(A\) (losing expressivity). FedRot keeps both factors trainable and instead reduces the error by aligning the rotation gauge. FFA-LoRA is a baseline in Table 1.
FLoRA stacks client factors for exact aggregation at rank \(Nr\) and higher communication. FedRot keeps rank \(r\) and communication unchanged (cited in related work; not a Table 1 baseline).

Structural analogue, not a baseline: KnOTS aligns several task LoRAs in a shared SVD basis before merging, FedRot aligns each client's factors to the previous global adapter by a Procrustes rotation before averaging. FedRot does not cite KnOTS.

methods.verification_notes: arXiv export API (fetched 2026-10-02): title, first author and first-version date match; HF PEFT main 9146289 (v0.21.2, 2026-10-01) src/peft/tuners has no tuner, init option or helper for this method; Semantic Scholar citation count matches the file notes. Venue: ICML 2026 poster 66566, 'Accept (regular)' in icml-2026-orals-posters.json; OpenReview forum 2X8Qi3VdjA is the paper_url in that record; arXiv comment 'ICML 2026'. Formula checked against Section 3 (Eqs. 3-6) and Algorithm 1 of arXiv v3: odd rounds align \(A\), even rounds align \(B\), reference is the previous global adapter, aggregation is uniform \(1/N\) averaging. Eq. 4, \(R^*=V\,\mathrm{diag}(1,\dots,\det(UV^\top))\,U^\top\) with \(M=A_{ref}A_i^\top=U\Sigma V^\top\), is the correct Procrustes solution. The soft-rotation projection reuses the same formula for \(R'=U\Sigma V^\top\), which gives the transpose of the nearest rotation; the released rotation_alignment_tools.py builds \(M=A_iA_{ref}^\top\), takes \(R=UV^\top\) and projects \(R'\) by \(U'V'^\top\), the nearest-rotation projection, so the entry's generic \(\Pi_{SO(r)}\) is right. Results checked against Table 1 (\(N=50\) block). Parameter count re-derived: \(r(d_{in}+d_{out})\) per adapted matrix, rotation computed in closed form.

Relation notes to ffa-lora, flora-federated and knots: stated which are baselines, which are only cited, and that KnOTS is a structural analogue that FedRot does not cite.

methods.name: LoRA-RLPO / LoRA-RLMO
methods.full_name: Geometry-preserving orthonormal LoRA initialization for RLVR (principal / minor variants)
methods.paper_title: Geometry-Preserving Orthonormal Initialization for Low-Rank Adaptation in RLVR
methods.formula_latex: W_0=U\Sigma V^\top;\quad h=\big(W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\big)x,\quad B_0=0_{d_{out}\times r},\quad A_0=V_{[:,1:r]}^\top\ (\text{LoRA-RLPO, top-}r)\ \ \text{or}\ \ A_0=V_{[:,-r:]}^\top\ (\text{LoRA-RLMO, bottom-}r),\ \ A_0A_0^\top=I_r;\quad \max_{A,B}\ \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta}[R(x,y)]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{ref})\ \ (\text{general RLVR objective, Eq. 9; the main DAPO runs drop the explicit KL term; GRPO for Qwen2.5-7B});\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen and not modified (no residual)},\ A,B\ \text{trained};\quad \tfrac1T\|W_T^{LoRA}-W_T^{full}\|_F\le M\eta\,\Gamma_T(\eta)\,\|I_{d_{in}}-A_0^\top A_0\|_2+O(\eta^2),\ \ \|I_{d_{in}}-A_0^\top A_0\|_2=\max\big(1,\max_i|1-s_i(A_0)^2|\big)\ge1\ \text{for } r<d_{in},\ \text{with equality iff every singular value } s_i(A_0)\le\sqrt2\ (\text{in particular if } A_0A_0^\top=I_r)
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix (}r=16\text{ in the main experiments)}
methods.locus: all linear layers (attention and MLP projections). Main runs: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with DAPO on DAPO-Math-17k (\(r=16\), \(\alpha=32\)). Appendix: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with GRPO (\(r=32\)), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on MBPP-style code generation, and an SFT check on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (GLUE CoLA and MRPC, GSM8K)
methods.structure: Plain rank-\(r\) LoRA \(\Delta W=\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\); only the starting point changes. \(A_0\) is the transpose of \(r\) right singular vectors of \(W_0\) (top \(r\) for RLPO, bottom \(r\) for RLMO), so it has orthonormal rows and no singular-value scaling, and \(B_0=0\). PiSSA and MiLoRA use \(B_0=U_r\Sigma_r^{1/2}\), \(A_0=\Sigma_r^{1/2}V_r^\top\) and a residual base \(W_0-B_0A_0\).
methods.mergeable_reason: After training, \(\tfrac{\alpha}{r}BA\) is an ordinary rank-\(r\) matrix added to the untouched \(W_0\).
methods.identity_at_init: Exact: \(B_0=0\) gives \(\Delta W=0\), and \(W_0\) is left untouched, unlike PiSSA, MiLoRA and OLoRA, which subtract \(B_0A_0\) from \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: In RLVR with \(B_0=0\), Theorem 5.2 bounds the gap between LoRA and full fine-tuning after \(T\) steps by a term proportional to \(\|I-A_0^\top A_0\|_2\ge1\). A row-orthonormal \(A_0\) attains this minimum and also caps the first update at full fine-tuning's (\(\|\Delta W_1\|_F\le\eta\|G_0\|_F\), Proposition 5.3). The minimum is not unique: any \(A_0\) whose singular values are at most \(\sqrt2\) attains it, including, with high probability, the \(\mathcal N(0,1/n)\) LoRA baseline in Table 1, so the bound alone does not separate orthonormal from Gaussian \(A_0\). Taking \(A_0\) from \(W_0\)'s principal or minor right singular vectors keeps PiSSA's and MiLoRA's subspaces but drops their singular-value scaling, which inflates the first update by at least \(\sigma_r\) (Theorem 4.1), and their nonzero \(B_0\). The authors argue this scaling explains the KL blow-up and reward collapse of PiSSA and MiLoRA in RL.
methods.results_note: With DAPO on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (\(r=16\), cosine LR, Table 1), LoRA-RLPO averages 65.03% over GSM8K, MATH500 and AIME22-24, versus 63.76% for LoRA-RLMO, 62.40% for LoRA, 51.71% for MiLoRA and 4.57% for PiSSA.

relations.note: Keeps LoRA's \(B_0=0\) and replaces the Gaussian \(A_0\) with an orthonormal, SVD-derived one.

RLPO uses the same top-\(r\) singular subspace without \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) scaling, without a nonzero \(B_0\) and without a residual base; PiSSA collapses under RLVR in the paper's runs (4.57% average in Table 1).

RLMO is the minor-subspace counterpart with orthonormal \(A_0\) and \(B_0=0\); the paper attributes MiLoRA's RLVR instability to singular-value scaling, not to near-zero tail initialization (Appendix D.1).

The paper uses an 'OLoRA' control with \(B_0=U_r\), \(A_0=V_r^\top\) and a residual base (Eq. 7), and proves PiSSA's first update is at least \(\sigma_r\) times that control's (Theorem 4.1). Published OLoRA (and HF PEFT init_lora_weights='olora') instead uses the QR factors \(B_0=Q_{[:,1:r]}\), \(A_0=R_{[1:r,:]}\), so the control is an SVD-orthonormal variant, not OLoRA as published. RLPO goes further and sets \(B_0=0\).
Cites the asymmetry result that a fixed random orthonormal \(A\) works well, and gives an RLVR-specific reason to prefer an orthonormal \(A_0\).

Both target the minor singular subspace of \(W_0\). MiCA freezes \(B=U_{[:,-r:]}\) and zero-initializes \(A\); RLMO sets \(A_0=V_{[:,-r:]}^\top\), \(B_0=0\) and trains both factors. MiCA is not cited.

Gives a theoretical account of that benchmark's finding that PiSSA and MiLoRA underperform LoRA and become unstable under RLVR, and disputes its near-zero-initialization explanation for MiLoRA (Appendix D.1).

methods.name: NaRA
methods.paper_title: NaRA: Noise-Aware LoRA for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Diffusion LLMs
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+B\,C(\lambda)\,A\,x,\quad C(\lambda)=I_r+\eta\,\mathcal{F}_\phi(e_\lambda),\quad e_\lambda=\cos(2\pi k\lambda)\oplus\sin(2\pi k\lambda),\ k\in\mathbb{R}^{32},\ k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2I)\ \text{fixed};\quad \lambda=m/L_s\in[0,1]\ (\text{fraction of masked response tokens});\quad \Delta W_{l,m}(\lambda)=B_{l,m}\,C(\lambda)\,A_{l,m},\ \ B_{l,m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A_{l,m}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ A,B\ (\text{per module})\ \text{and one globally shared MLP}\ \mathcal{F}_\phi:\mathbb{R}^{64}\to\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}\ \text{trained};\ \eta=0.1
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix} + |\phi|\ \text{once per model (shared MLP } 64\to256\to512\to r^2;\ \approx6.7\times10^{5}\ \text{for } r=32)
methods.locus: q, k, v, o attention projections of masked-diffusion LLMs (LLaDA-8B-Base and LLaDA-8B-Instruct); one image-diffusion experiment (SDXL, DreamBooth) in Section 6.6
methods.structure: \(\Delta W(\lambda)=BC(\lambda)A\). Static per-module factors \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\) sandwich a dynamic \(r\times r\) core that is a smooth function of the scalar noise level \(\lambda\). One Fourier-feature MLP, shared by every adapted module, produces the core once per denoising step. The update therefore moves continuously along the denoising trajectory inside fixed rank-\(r\) column and row spaces.
methods.mergeable_reason: For a fixed \(\lambda\), \(W_0+BC(\lambda)A\) is a dense matrix. But \(\lambda\) changes at every denoising step (and can differ across sequences in a batch), so no single merged weight exists. The paper lists non-mergeability as a limitation (Appendix, Table 10); re-merging at every step is possible in principle (catalogue's inference, not the paper's).
methods.identity_at_init: \(B=0\) gives \(\Delta W(\lambda)=0\) for every \(\lambda\). The hypernetwork's last layer is zero-initialized, so \(C(\lambda)=I_r\) and the initial gradients equal LoRA's.
methods.key_idea: Masked-diffusion LLMs see very different inputs at different noise levels, so a static \(\Delta W\) helps mostly at mid noise. NaRA sandwiches a noise-conditioned core \(C(\lambda)=I_r+\eta\mathcal F_\phi(e_\lambda)\) between static LoRA factors, giving a continuous family \(\Delta W(\lambda)\). Theorem 4.1 shows this family can represent any finite set of updates whose combined column and row spaces have dimension \(\le r\); the extra parameters are under 0.01% of the model. Timestep-conditioned LoRAs already existed for image diffusion (TC-LoRA, TimeStep Master); NaRA is the first noise-aware PEFT for diffusion LLMs.
methods.results_note: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct commonsense reasoning (\(r=32\), Table 1), NaRA averages 84.09% versus 80.18% for LoRA and 82.73% for HiRA, with 0.425% versus 0.417% trainable parameters.

relations.note: \(\eta=0\) (so \(C=I_r\)) recovers LoRA exactly.

Structural comparison (MoSLoRA is not cited). A \(\lambda\)-independent hypernetwork output gives a static \(r\times r\) core between \(B\) and \(A\), but NaRA's core is shared by every adapted module, whereas MoSLoRA learns one mixer per module, so neither method contains the other. Only the module-specific hypernetwork ablation (Section 6.3) would contain MoSLoRA.
Strongest baseline on commonsense reasoning (82.73% vs NaRA's 84.09%, Table 1). On mathematical reasoning (Table 2) plain LoRA and P-Tuning beat HiRA.
Appendix M applies the same noise-conditioned core inside DoRA.

methods.name: LiME
methods.paper_title: LiME: Lightweight Mixture of Experts for Efficient Multimodal Multi-task Learning
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\hat z\odot\mathcal{P}(x)+\gamma\,(\hat z\odot p_s),\quad \hat z=\delta_\phi(x)\ (\text{e.g. } \tfrac{\alpha}{r}BAx,\ r=2,\ \alpha=4),\quad \mathcal{P}(x)=\sum_{i\in S_\theta(x)}\tilde w_i(x)\,p_i,\ \ p_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}};\quad w(x)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\tfrac{(1-\gamma_r)\,z_{1:E}/\|z_{1:E}\|_\infty+\gamma_r\,\hat z_{1:E}/\|\hat z_{1:E}\|_\infty}{\tau}\Big),\ \ z=W_0x;\quad S_\theta(x)=\{i:w_i(x)\ge\theta\max_jw_j(x)\},\ \ \tilde w_i=w_i\big/\textstyle\sum_{j\in S_\theta}w_j;\ \ W_0\ \text{frozen};\ \phi,\{p_i\},p_s,\gamma\ \text{trained};\ \text{router has no parameters};\ \ \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{task}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{imp}+\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\bar p\,\|\,\mathcal{U});\ \ \text{defaults: } E=4,\ \gamma_r=0.7,\ \tau=0.5,\ \theta=0.7,\ n\text{-gram window }3
methods.trainable_params: |\phi|+E\,d_{out}+d_{out}+1\ \text{per adapted layer (LoRA: } |\phi|=r(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{), versus } E|\phi|\ \text{plus a } d\times E \text{ router for MoE-LoRA}
methods.locus: q, k, v, o attention projections in both the SigLIP vision encoder and the Qwen2 LLM of LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2-7B (216 target layers; 0.5B model for ablations; also Molmo2-8B); wraps LoRA, DoRA, LoRA-FA, SliceFine (\(r=2\), \(\alpha=4\)) or prompt tuning (10 virtual tokens); \(E=4\) experts, n-gram routing window 3
methods.structure: The output \(\hat z\) of one shared PEFT module is rescaled element-wise by a convex combination of \(E\) expert vectors. A parameter-free softmax router chooses the combination from normalized slices of \(W_0x\) and \(\hat z\), with confidence-adaptive top-\(k\) and one decision per n-gram window. For LoRA this is \(\Delta W(x)=\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal P(x)+\gamma p_s)\,BA\): a token-dependent diagonal rescaling of the rows of one rank-\(r\) update.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\mathcal P(x)\) depends on each token (or n-gram window) through the router, so \(\Delta W(x)=\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal P(x)+\gamma p_s)BA\) varies per token. Only with \(E=1\) does it collapse to a static, mergeable \(\mathrm{diag}(p_1+\gamma p_s)BA\).
methods.identity_at_init: With LoRA, the released code zero-initializes \(B\), so \(\hat z=0\) and \(h=W_0x\) exactly. Initialization is \(p_i\sim\mathcal U(0.9,1.1)\), \(p_s\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2)\), \(\gamma=0\), so LiME also starts close to the plain shared PEFT module.
methods.key_idea: MoE-PEFT methods normally keep \(E\) adapter copies plus a learned router. LiME keeps one PEFT module and lets \(E\) vectors \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}}\) rescale its output, so expert cost becomes \(E\,d_{out}\) and works with any PEFT method. Routing logits come for free from the first \(E\) coordinates of the frozen output and the PEFT output. Theorem 2 states that the optimal-risk gap to expert-specific PEFT is \(O(\bar\varepsilon)\) if the modulation approximates it within \(\bar\varepsilon\); the approximation error itself is assumed, not bounded.
methods.results_note: On MMT-47 with LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2-7B (Table 2), LiME-LoRA has the best commonsense-reasoning average (84.98%), with 3.49M trainable parameters versus 10.79M for MoELoRA. In the GLUE efficiency study (one epoch on one H100, about 894M total parameters), LiME-LoRA trains 0.52M parameters versus 1.97M for MoELoRA and runs 23% faster.

relations.note: Structural competitor: MOELoRA (2310.18339) replicates LoRA experts under a task-id gate. LiME does not cite it; LiME's 'MoELoRA' baseline is a different paper, Luo et al. 2024 (arXiv 2402.12851), which the catalogue does not list. Against that baseline LiME uses 3-4 times fewer trainable parameters.
HydraLoRA shares \(A\) and routes among several \(B\) heads. LiME shares the whole adapter and routes among diagonal output scalings. HydraLoRA is a Table 2 baseline.
MoE-PEFT baseline with replicated LoRA experts and a learned router.
Cited as an adapter-replicating MoE-PEFT design.
MoV already mixes routed (IA)\(^3\) scaling vectors with a learned router. LiME applies routed scaling vectors to a shared PEFT output and removes the router. LiME does not cite MoV.
LiME-LoRA.
LiME-DoRA.
LiME-LoRA-FA.
LiME-PromptTuning shows the wrapper also works for non-adapter PEFT.

methods.locus: all parameters (full-parameter zeroth-order fine-tuning); activation-guided perturbations on linear layers (attention and FFN projections), dense Gaussian perturbations elsewhere; Qwen3-0.6B/4B and openPangu-Embedded-1B, plus Qwen3-8B in the appendix
methods.structure: A randomized finite-difference (SPSA) gradient estimate with rank-\(r\) perturbations \(R_\ell U_\ell^\top\). Their row space is the top-\(r\) left singular subspace of the layer's current input activations. In expectation the estimate is \(\nabla_{W_\ell}F_{\mu,U}(W)\,U_\ell U_\ell^\top\): the gradient of a subspace-smoothed objective, projected onto the activation subspace.
methods.mergeable_reason: AGZO edits the model's own weights in place; there is no adapter to merge.
methods.identity_at_init: Trivial: there is no reparameterization, and training starts at \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: A linear layer's gradient \(Q_\ell H_\ell^\top\) has its row space inside the span of the layer's input activations, and that span is spectrally concentrated. AGZO therefore perturbs only along \(R_\ell U_\ell^\top\), with \(U_\ell\) the top activation directions found by power iteration in the same forward pass. The expected cosine with the true gradient is \(\beta_{d_{out}r}\|GU\|_F/\|G\|_F\), versus \(\beta_{d_{out}d_{in}}\) for MeZO (Theorem 5.4, Corollary 5.5). Theorem 5.6 makes the gain strict when the activations are rank-deficient and the average upstream-gradient energy along the top-\(r\) activation directions is at least the average over all of them.
methods.results_note: On Qwen3-0.6B, AGZO beats MeZO and LOZO on most SuperGLUE-style tasks, e.g. CB 0.892 versus 0.803 (MeZO) and 0.760 (LOZO), against 0.946 for first-order fine-tuning, with almost the same peak memory as MeZO.

relations.note: With \(U_\ell=I\) (full activation space) the estimator has MeZO's dense Gaussian form (Corollary 5.5), up to AGZO's one-sided versus MeZO's two-sided finite difference.

Both confine updates to a data-derived low-rank subspace. GaLore uses the gradient's top singular vectors (first-order); AGZO uses the activations', which contain the gradient's row space (zeroth-order). AGZO does not cite GaLore.

Both use low-rank ZO perturbations. AGZO's subspace is activation-informed on the input side; ZO-Muon's is random on the output side and adds Muon-style orthogonalization. Neither paper cites the other.
The released code is built on the ZO-LLM benchmark codebase.

methods.name: ZO-Muon
methods.full_name: Zeroth-order Muon via subspace gradient orthogonalization
methods.paper_title: Powering Up Zeroth-Order Training via Subspace Gradient Orthogonalization
methods.formula_latex: \text{for each weight } W_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}}:\ P_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ P_\ell^\top P_\ell=I_r\ (\text{QR of a Gaussian, resampled every } v=100 \text{ steps});\quad \widehat G_{Z,\ell}=\frac{1}{N_q}\sum_{i=1}^{N_q}\frac{f(W+\mu P\Psi_i)-f(W)}{\mu}\,\Psi_{i,\ell},\ \ \Psi_{i,\ell}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{r\times d_{in}});\quad O_\ell=P_\ell\,\mathrm{msign}(\widehat G_{Z,\ell}),\ \ \mathrm{msign}(G)=(GG^\top)^{-1/2}G=U_kV_k^\top\ \text{for } G\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\ (\text{the paper's } G(G^\top G)^{-1/2} \text{ needs a pseudo-inverse here; computed by Newton--Schulz});\quad W_\ell\leftarrow W_\ell-\eta\,O_\ell;\ \ \text{first-order analogue } O=P\,\mathrm{msign}(P^\top\nabla_Wf),\ \text{equal to } \mathrm{msign}(\nabla_Wf) \text{ when } P \text{ spans the gradient's column space};\ \text{all weights trained, no backpropagation; 1-D parameters (biases, norms) use dense Gaussian RGE};\ N_q=4,\ r\in\{64,128\}\ \text{for LLMs};\ N_q=16,\ r=64\ \text{for ViTs}
methods.trainable_params: \text{all } d_{out}d_{in} \text{ entries of each weight matrix (full-parameter ZO); each step's update has rank} \le r;\ \text{state: } P_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}
methods.locus: all weight matrices (full-parameter zeroth-order fine-tuning) of OPT-1.3B/13B, LLaMA3-8B and Gemma2-2B (SuperGLUE, SQuAD) and ViT-B/16, ViT-L/16 (CIFAR-10/100)
methods.structure: A multi-query forward-difference gradient estimate (RGE) is taken in a random rank-\(r\) left subspace \(\mathrm{col}(P)\), which is lazily resampled. The \(r\times d_{in}\) estimate is orthogonalized by the matrix sign function and lifted back by \(P\). With an exact matrix sign each update \(P\,\mathrm{msign}(\widehat G_Z)\) is a rank-\(\le r\) partial isometry whose nonzero singular values equal 1; the Newton–Schulz iteration used in practice makes them only approximately 1.
methods.mergeable_reason: ZO-Muon edits the model's own weights in place; there is no adapter to merge.
methods.identity_at_init: Trivial: there is no reparameterization, and training starts at \(W_0\).
methods.key_idea: Estimate the ZO gradient of the projected variable \(Z\) (\(W\approx PZ\), with \(P\) random and column-orthonormal) by multi-query RGE. This cuts the dimension behind the estimator's variance from \(d_{out}d_{in}\) to \(rd_{in}\). Then orthogonalize the estimate Muon-style and lift it back with \(P\). Orthogonalizing full-space MeZO estimates (ZO-Muon-V0) does not help, but inside the subspace the matrix sign acts as a spectral noise filter, making ZO-Muon a zeroth-order approximation of low-rank Muon.
methods.results_note: Versus MeZO, ZO-Muon needs 24.7% of the queries to reach 0.90 on SST-2 (OPT-1.3B, Fig. 2a) and reaches 72.4% versus 47.3% on CIFAR-100 with ViT-L (Table 1). The abstract attributes this +25.1-point gain to ViT-B, but Table 1 shows it is ViT-L.

relations.note: Same seed-regenerated, forward-only RGE. ZO-Muon adds a random orthonormal subspace, multiple queries and Muon-style orthogonalization; applying \(\mathrm{msign}\) to MeZO directly (ZO-Muon-V0) fails.

Zeroth-order counterpart of projected low-rank updates with periodic subspace refresh (GaLore is cited). GaLore uses gradient SVD; ZO-Muon uses a random \(P\), since informed sketches gave no gain (Table A3).
Both rely on a random projection that is resampled periodically, rather than a learned subspace, to keep low-rank optimizer state cheap. Flora is cited.
Low-rank ZO with a random output-side subspace plus orthogonalization, versus AGZO's activation-informed input-side subspace. Neither paper cites the other.

notes: Scope: one entry per requested method; all six exist, are distinct from catalogued ids, and are PEFT or memory-efficient-fine-tuning methods. None was skipped. VENUES checked against https://icml.cc/static/virtual/data/icml-2026-orals-posters.json on 2026-10-02: FedRot-LoRA (poster 66566), Geometry-Preserving Orthonormal Init / RLPO-RLMO (poster 63355), NaRA (poster 61250) and AGZO (poster 60499) are 'Accept (regular)'; LiME (poster 64728) is 'Accept (spotlight)'. ZO-Muon is not in the ICLR 2026, ICML 2026 or NeurIPS 2026 accepted lists (checked 2026-10-02 by title and first author) and its arXiv comment field is empty, so its venue is arXiv. Semantic Scholar citations (2026-10-02): ZO-Muon 11 (3 influential), FedRot-LoRA 9 (1), AGZO 3 (1), RLPO-RLMO 1, NaRA 1, LiME 0. Suggested site families: fedrot-lora -> lora-core (federated aggregation; also gap-3 next to ffa-lora and flora-federated); rlpo-rlmo -> init-rank; nara -> frontier; lime -> composition; agzo and zo-muon -> quant-memory. HF PEFT v0.21.2 (2026-10-01) has no tuner or init option for any of the six. Its LoraConfig(init_lora_weights='orthogonal') is a different, data-free scheme: both factors are nonzero, with BA=0 via orthogonal row splitting, so it is NOT RLPO. DISCREPANCIES AND CAVEATS: (1) ZO-Muon: the abstract says '+25.1% on ViT-B CIFAR-100', but Table 1 and Section 5.2 give 72.4 vs 47.3 for ViT-L (ViT-B is 72.6 vs 64.5). The results_note follows the table. (2) FedRot-LoRA: the paper's soft-rotation projection formula writes V diag(.) U^T for R' = U Sigma V^T, the transpose of the nearest rotation. The released code (rotation_alignment_tools.py) uses U' V'^T and builds M = A A_ref^T, consistent with R = U V^T. The formula entry therefore writes a generic projection onto SO(r). Uniform 1/N averaging as in Algorithm 1. (3) NaRA: the 'first noise-conditioned LoRA' claim holds only for diffusion LLMs. Timestep-conditioned LoRAs already exist for image diffusion: TC-LoRA (2510.09561, hypernetwork-generated per-step LoRA, earlier excluded from the catalogue) and TimeStep Master (timestep-interval LoRA experts). NaRA's architecture is credited to Terra (Time-Varying LoRA, NeurIPS 2024, same group), whose variable is a domain-flow time rather than the noise level. NaRA's hypernetwork size (about 0.67M) is computed from Table 12 (64->256->512->1024, biases assumed), not stated in the paper. (4) LiME: arXiv id 2604.02338 although the v1 timestamp is 2026-02-01. The repo README badge text shows a different id (2510.08513 = SliceFine), but its link points to 2604.02338. Initial values of B, p_s and gamma are from the paper's hyperparameter table and the released LiMELoRA.py; the paper (Appendix J) adds multiplicative routing jitter (sigma=0.1) during training; in the released code it is off by default (jitter_noise=0.0) and enabled via set_jitter. LiME's 'MoELoRA' baseline is Luo et al. 2024 (2402.12851), not the catalogue's MOELoRA (2310.18339). (5) AGZO renames the activation basis A_l to U_l here to avoid a clash with the LoRA factor A. The power iteration Y=H Omega; repeat qr then Y=H(H^T Q) spans (HH^T)^K H Omega. The official repo is LouisLINWEI/AGZO (code described as a rough draft) plus an NPU fork. (6) RLPO/RLMO: experiments use alpha=32, r=16 (alpha/r=2), but the theorem is stated for unscaled BA. Its minimum ||I - A_0^T A_0||_2 = 1 is reached by any A_0 with singular values at most sqrt(2), not only by orthonormal A_0. The paper's 'OLoRA' control (B_0=U_r, A_0=V_r^T) is not published OLoRA, which uses QR factors. The ablation shows orthonormality alone (DCT-LoRA, Wavelet-LoRA) beats LoRA, while principal-subspace geometry adds a further gain only for RLPO. TENSION WORTH TAGGING: AGZO finds that a data-informed (activation) subspace improves ZO gradient alignment, while ZO-Muon reports that informed sketches (Gaussian sketching or past-gradient bases) give no gain over random P. They project on different sides (input vs output) and ZO-Muon adds orthogonalization, so the results are not directly contradictory. CATEGORY-THEORY NOTE: FedRot-LoRA is an explicit gauge fixing (choosing a representative in the SO(r) orbit of the GL(r) inner symmetry of (B, A)) applied before a non-equivariant operation (factor averaging). It belongs with learning-on-loras-gl-equivariance, balanced-lora and lora-rite as methods that treat the factorization's symmetry explicitly, but FedRot does not cite them.
verification_summary: Adversarial check on 2026-10-02 of all 6 methods (no papers) in addendum2026-1; all 6 confirmed and kept, none dropped. Metadata: the six arXiv ids were fetched one by one from the export API; titles, first authors (Zhang, Zhang, Wang, Kowsher, Lin, Lang) and first-version years (all 2026) match. Venues: FedRot-LoRA (66566), RLPO/RLMO (63355), NaRA (61250) and AGZO (60499) are 'Accept (regular)' and LiME (64728) 'Accept (spotlight)' in icml-2026-orals-posters.json, with matching OpenReview forum ids; ZO-Muon is absent from the ICLR, ICML and NeurIPS 2026 lists and stays arXiv. Formulas were checked against the method sections of the latest arXiv HTML versions and, where code was cited, against the released code (FedRot rotation_alignment_tools.py, LiMELoRA.py, ZO-Muon LowDimTrainer.py, AGZO README). HF PEFT main 9146289 / v0.21.2: no tuner, init option or helper for any of the six (hf_peft stays false). All ids are new against existing_index.json, and all 33 relation targets resolve to existing ids or to ids in this file. Substantive fixes: (1) RLPO's 'equality iff orthonormal' was wrong (equality iff all singular values of A_0 are at most sqrt(2), which also covers Gaussian LoRA init); the paper's 'OLoRA' control is SVD-based, not published QR-based OLoRA; DAPO runs have no explicit KL term. (2) LiME's relation to moelora described a different paper (LiME's MoELoRA baseline is 2402.12851); efficiency figures were attributed to the right experiment; the vision encoder is also adapted (r=2, alpha=4); Theorem 2 is conditional. (3) NaRA -> moslora retyped from generalizes to competes-with (NaRA's core is shared across modules); the HiRA note is limited to commonsense. (4) ZO-Muon's msign formula was rewritten in the well-defined wide-matrix form; the partial-isometry claim is exact only for an exact msign. (5) FedRot's init statement now follows Algorithm 1; AGZO's dominance condition now follows Theorem 5.6. Math in prose fields (structure, key_idea, identity_at_init, mergeable_reason, results_note, locus, relation notes) is wrapped in \( \). Mergeable, identity_at_init, modification_kind and trainable_params were re-derived and left unchanged.
